## This tutorial: Forecasting with AR-GARCH {auto-animate="true"}


<blue>In this tutorial, we use an AR-GARCH model to generate ex-ante forecasts of S&P 500 returns and volatilities, and investigate whether non-normality materially affects forecasting performance.</blue>

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div> 

:::{.callout-note title="Activities"} 

- <blue>Exercise 1:</blue> Understanding R output
- <blue>Exercise 2:</blue> Event Matching with estimated volatility series 
- <blue>Exercise 3:</blue> Investigating the distributional properties of return series and standardised residuals 
- <blue>Exercise 4:</blue> Constructing point forecasts and normal prediction intervals 
- <blue>Exercise 5:</blue> Using bootstrapping to build empirical prediction intervals and comparing them with the normal case 

:::


## Initialisation

<blue>In Self-Directed Activities 10, you have carried out a model specification exercise for the S&P 500 returns time series that comes with the `rugarch` package.

You arrived at an AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) specification.</blue>
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
Please install the R packages `rugarch` and `moments` before proceeding:
```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages("rugarch")
install.packages("moments")
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
Set up as follows:
```{r}
library(rugarch)
library(moments)
data("sp500ret")
Y <- sp500ret$SP500RET*100

h <- 5
n <- length(Y)-h
Yf <- ts(Y[(n+1):length(Y)], start=n+1)
Y <- ts(Y[1:n], start=1, end=n)

AR4GARCH11 <- ugarchfit(data=Y,
    ugarchspec(variance.model=list(garchOrder=c(1,1)),
               mean.model=list(armaOrder=c(4,0))))
```

## Exercise 1 {auto-animate="true"}

:::{.callout-question}
Write out the full set of estimated mean and variance equations that constitute this model.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

The estimated coefficients can be obtained as follows:
```{r}
print(round(coef(AR4GARCH11), 3))
```

:::{.fragment}
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
The estimated AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) model is therefore:
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=0.052+\widehat{Z}_{t}\\
\widehat{Z}_{t}&=-0.01\widehat{Z}_{t-1}-0.015\widehat{Z}_{t-2}-0.019\widehat{Z}_{t-3}-0.043\widehat{Z}_{t-4}+\widehat{U}_{t}\\
\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}&=0.014+0.089\widehat{U}^{2}_{t-1}+0.904\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t-1}
\end{align}
:::


## Exercise 2 {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
Obtain the time series of estimated standard deviations, denoted $\widehat{\sigma}_{t}=\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(U_{t}^{2}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t-1})}$, implied by the model. Plot this series.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
AR4GARCH11_sigma <- ts(sigma(AR4GARCH11), start=1, end=n)

plot(AR4GARCH11_sigma, 
     main = "Estimated SD series from AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) model",
     ylab = "Standard Deviation")
```

## Exercise 3(a) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
(a) Compute the mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis of the return series `Y`. The R commands `mean` and `sd` are standard, while `skewness` and `kurtosis` are obtained from the `moments` package.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
:::{.incremental}
- The skewness and kurtosis are standard descriptive statistics given by:
$$\text{Skewness}=\frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{t=1}(Y_{t}-\bar{Y})^{3}}{s^{3}};\quad\text{Kurtosis}=\frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{t=1}(Y_{t}-\bar{Y})^{4}}{s^{4}}$$
where $s$ is the sample standard deviation.

- <blue>Skewness:</blue> 
  - $\text{Skewness}=0$ if the distribution is symmetric; 
  - $\text{Skewness}>0$ if right-skewed;
  - $\text{Skewness}<0$ if left-skewed.

- <blue>Kurtosis:</blue> Measure of "tail thickness"

  - When $\text{Kurtosis}>3$, the tails are "fatter" than a normal distribution (more outliers).
:::


## Exercise 3(a) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
(a) Compute the mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis of the return series `Y`. The R commands `mean` and `sd` are standard, while `skewness` and `kurtosis` are obtained from the `moments` package.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.panel-tabset}

## Moments
```{r}
stats_Y = c(mean(Y), sd(Y), skewness(Y), kurtosis(Y))
names(stats_Y) <- c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "kurtosis")
print(round(stats_Y, 3))
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>

- The mean return is slightly positive (share prices having a long term overall tendency to increase over this period). 

- The skewness is negative ($-1.541$) and kurtosis of $\approx 36$ very much greater than 3, implying non-normality. 

- Both skewness and kurtosis will be inflated in magnitude by the large negative outlier for the 1987 crash, as well as some of the other outliers.

## Histogram
```{r}
hist(Y, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, main = "Daily Returns on SP500 (%)")
x <- seq(from=-10, to=10, length.out=100)
lines(x, dnorm(x, mean=mean(Y), sd = sd(Y)), col="red", lwd=2)
```


::: {.absolute top="620px" left="370px" style="font-size: 32px;"}
<red>$\mathrm{N}(0.019, 1.193^2)$</red>
:::

::: {.absolute top="530px" left="910px" style="font-size: 32px;"}
The large kurtosis is evident in the long tails of the histogram, counterbalanced by the taller than normal peak around the mean.
:::

:::


## Exercise 3(b) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
(b) Obtain the standard residuals $\widehat{U}_{t}^*$ from the AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) model, and investigate their distribution in the same way as part (a).
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.fragment}
:::{.callout-tip}
In a general AR($p$)-GARCH(1,1) model of the form
\begin{align}
Y_{t}&=\mu +Z_{t}\\
Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\cdots+\phi_{p}Z_{t-p}+U_{t}\\
\sigma_{t}^{2}&=\omega+\alpha_{1}U_{t-1}^{2}+\gamma_{1}\sigma^{2}_{t-1}
\end{align}

where $\sigma^{2}=\operatorname{var}(U_{t}\mid \mathscr{Y}_{t-1})$, the *standardised prediction errors $U_{t}^*$*
$$U_{t}^{*}=\frac{U_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}$$
will be <green>conditionally homoskedastic</green>, assuming the model is well specified:
$$\operatorname{var}(U_{t}^*\mid\mathscr{Y}_{t-1})=1$$

:::
<div style="height: 0.2em;"></div>
:::

:::{.fragment}
<blue>The distribution of these standardised prediction errors determines the distribution that is appropriate for the prediction intervals.</blue>
:::

:::{.incremental}
- If $U_{t}^*$ is normally distributed then the normal prediction intervals will be correct.

- Otherwise, the normal prediction intervals may be only approximate and not have the required 95% coverage property.
:::


## Exercise 3(b) {auto-animate="true"}
:::{.callout-question}
(b) Obtain the standard residuals $\widehat{U}_{t}^*$ from the AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) model, and investigate their distribution in the same way as part (a).
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r}
Us <- residuals(AR4GARCH11, standardize = TRUE)
```

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.panel-tabset}

## Moments
```{r}
stats_Us = c(mean(Us), sd(Us), skewness(Us), kurtosis(Us))
names(stats_Us) <- c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "kurtosis")
print(round(stats_Us, 3))
```

<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
The descriptive statistics and histogram reveal that the residuals retain clear signs of non-normality <teal>(some negative skewness and substantial excess kurtosis)</teal> although these are reduced relative to the same measures for the original data series.

## Histogram
```{r}
hist(Us, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, 
     main = "AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) Standardised Residuals")
x <- seq(from=-10, to=5, length.out=100)
lines(x, dnorm(x, mean=mean(Us), sd = sd(Us)), col="red", lwd=2)
```
::: {.absolute top="620px" left="380px" style="font-size: 32px;"}
<red>$\mathrm{N}(0.035, 0.999^2)$</red>
:::


::: {.absolute top="560px" left="800px" style="font-size: 32px;"}
It is commonly the case with GARCH models that the standardised residuals are closely to normality than the original data, but still not close to approximately normal.
:::

:::


## Exercise 4
:::{.callout-question}
From the AR(4)-GARCH(1,1) model, obtain the point/mean forecasts for `Y` for 5 days into the future (one business week), the standard deviation for the forecasts, and the 95% normal prediction intervals. 
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
:::{.panel-tabset}

## Code

```{r eval=FALSE}
AR4GARCH11f <- ugarchforecast(AR4GARCH11, n.ahead=h)

Point <- ts(c(fitted(AR4GARCH11f)), start=n+1, end=n+h)
Sigma <- ts(c(sigma(AR4GARCH11f)), start=n+1, end=n+h)
Lower <- ts(Point-1.96*Sigma, start=n+1, end=n+h)
Upper <- ts(Point+1.96*Sigma, start=n+1, end=n+h)

AR4GARCH11Forecasts <- data.frame(
                          Lower=round(Lower,3),
                          Point=round(Point,3),
                          Upper=round(Upper,3),
                          Actual=round(Yf,3),
                          Error=round(Yf-Point,3),
                          Sigma=round(Sigma,3))

print(AR4GARCH11Forecasts, row.names=FALSE)
```

## Results and Discussions

```{r echo=FALSE}
AR4GARCH11f <- ugarchforecast(AR4GARCH11, n.ahead=h)

Point <- ts(c(fitted(AR4GARCH11f)), start=n+1, end=n+h)
Sigma <- ts(c(sigma(AR4GARCH11f)), start=n+1, end=n+h)
Lower <- ts(Point-1.96*Sigma, start=n+1, end=n+h)
Upper <- ts(Point+1.96*Sigma, start=n+1, end=n+h)

AR4GARCH11Forecasts <- data.frame(
                          Lower=round(Lower,3),
                          Point=round(Point,3),
                          Upper=round(Upper,3),
                          Actual=round(Yf,3),
                          Error=round(Yf-Point,3),
                          Sigma=round(Sigma,3))

print(AR4GARCH11Forecasts, row.names=FALSE)
```

<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
:::{.callout-question}
Do the prediction intervals "cover" the actual values?
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>


<blue>Yes -</blue> In this case the actual value turns out to lie within the prediction interval at all of the 5 forecast days.

## Forecast Errors and RMSE

:::{.callout-question}
Also, compute the forecast errors and the RMSE.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>


```{r}
ForecastError <- Yf - Point
print(ForecastError)
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
RMSE <- sqrt(mean(ForecastError^2))
cat("The RMSE for the forecasts is", round(RMSE, 3), "\n")
```
:::


## Exercise 5 {auto-animate="true"}

:::{.callout-question}
Given the apparent non-normality of the model residuals, we may be motivated to compute the PIs using the bootstrap, rather than using the normal distribution critical values.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

[<blue>Bootstrapping: </blue>Constructing an empirical distribution by resampling from the data itself]{.fragment} [<teal>$\to$ treat the observed sample as if it were the population distribution</teal>]{.fragment}
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.fragment}
```{r}
AR4GARCH11fBS <- ugarchboot(AR4GARCH11, method="Partial", 
                        n.ahead=h, n.bootpred=5000)
```
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

:::{.fragment}
:::{.callout-note title="What is happening behind the scenes?"}

In each bootstrapping experiment, when `method="Partial"`:

:::{.incremental}
- Construct the residuals using the estimated parameters 

- Draw a bootstrapped sample (in our case, of length `n.ahead=h`), with replacement, from the observed set of residuals.

- Recalculate the forecasts given this sample and construct PIs.
:::

[The number of experiments is set under `n.bootpred=5000`.]{.fragment}
:::
:::

<div style="height: 0.2em;"></div>
:::{.fragment}
<blue>This allows us to focus on the difference between the normal and non-normal bootstrap intervals.</blue> [<green>It is also computationally quicker!</green>]{.fragment}
:::


## Exercise 5 {auto-animate="true"}

:::{.callout-question}
Given the apparent non-normality of the model residuals, we may be motivated to compute the PIs using the bootstrap, rather than using the normal distribution critical values.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

<blue>Bootstrapping: </blue>Constructing an empirical distribution by resampling from the data itself <teal>$\to$ treat the observed sample as if it were the population distribution</teal>
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>


```{r}
AR4GARCH11fBS <- ugarchboot(AR4GARCH11, method="Partial", 
                        n.ahead=h, n.bootpred=5000)
```

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>


:::{.callout-note title="What is happening behind the scenes?"}

In each bootstrapping experiment, when `method="Full"`:


- <teal>Draw a bootstrapped sample, with replacement, from the original data, and re-estimate the model parameters.</teal>

- Construct the residuals using the estimated parameters 

- Draw a bootstrapped sample (in our case, of length `n.ahead=h`), with replacement, from the observed set of residuals.

- Recalculate the forecasts given this sample and construct PIs.

The number of experiments is set under `n.bootpred=5000`.
:::



## Exercise 5 {auto-animate="true"}

:::{.callout-question}
Given the apparent non-normality of the model residuals, we may be motivated to compute the PIs using the bootstrap, rather than using the normal distribution critical values.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

```{r}
AR4GARCH11fBS <- ugarchboot(AR4GARCH11, method="Partial", 
                        n.ahead=h, n.bootpred=5000)
```

:::{.panel-tabset}

## Forecast Paths

The object produced by `ugarchboot` contains a matrix `fseries` of forecast series. Here, each row corresponds to a simulated forecast path, and there are 5000 of them.

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>


```{r}
print(AR4GARCH11fBS@fseries)
```


## Bootstrapped PIs
<div style="height: 0.3em;"></div>
Since bootstrapping involves randomness through data resampling, my prediction intervals should be similar to yours, though not exactly identical.
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
LowerBS <- apply(AR4GARCH11fBS@fseries, 2, quantile, probs=0.025)
UpperBS <- apply(AR4GARCH11fBS@fseries, 2, quantile, probs=0.975)
MedianBS <- apply(AR4GARCH11fBS@fseries, 2, quantile, probs=0.5)

print(round(cbind(LowerBS, UpperBS, MedianBS),3))
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

The median (50% quantile) is taken here as the "Point Forecast".

## Normal PIs (from Q3)
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
The Prediction Intervals and Point Forecasts (Mean) from Question 3 were included here for reference.
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
```{r}
NormalPI <- cbind(Lower, Upper, Point)
print(round(NormalPI,3))
```

## RMSE
Normal (<blue>Mean</blue> as point forecast)
```{r}
RMSE <- sqrt(mean(ForecastError^2))
print(RMSE)
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>


Bootstrapping (<teal>Median</teal> as point forecast)
```{r}
MedianErrors <- Yf-MedianBS
RMSE_Median <- sqrt(mean(MedianErrors^2))
print(RMSE_Median)
```

<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
<blue>The RMSE for the median is slightly different than that for the mean, although this should not be over-stated since the practical differences between the two sets of forecasts are clearly very small.</blue>


## Why Median?
Why we would consider the median instead of mean for forecasting, when we know the conditional mean is the optimal forecasting function?

- The conditional mean minimises the <blue>mean squared errors (MSE)</blue>:
$$\textsf{Mean Squared Error}=\frac{1}{h}\sum^{n+h}_{t=n+1}\widehat{U}_{t}^{2}$$

- The conditional median minimises the <blue>mean absolute errors (MAE)</blue>:
$$\textsf{Mean Absolute Error}=\frac{1}{h}\sum^{n+h}_{t=n+1}\left|\widehat{U}_{t}\right|$$


<div style="margin-top: -1em;"></div>
:::{.callout-note}
<blue>**Note:** The full model for the median would involve the estimation of *conditional quantiles*.</blue> Nevertheless, bootstrapping is an interesting sensitivity analysis for the importance of non-normality for the forecasts and intervals from the model.
:::


## MAE
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
We can compare the MAEs for the mean and median forecasts as follows, but there is little difference here because the forecasts themselves are so similar.
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>
Normal (<blue>Mean</blue> as point forecast)
```{r}
MAE_mean <- mean(abs(AR4GARCH11Forecasts$Error))
print(MAE_mean)
```
<div class="horizontal-line"></div>


Bootstrapping (<teal>Median</teal> as point forecast)
```{r}
MAE_median <- mean(abs(MedianErrors))
print(MAE_median)
```


## What matters for PIs?

:::{.callout-note}
In this case it might seem surprising that there is not a great difference between the bootstrap and normal prediction intervals, given that the standardised residuals are clearly non-normal (as shown in Question 3b).
:::

- While the skewness and kurtosis in 3(b) deviate from those from a normal distribution, these moments are not directly relevant for constructing PIs.

- Of direct relevance are the quantiles of the standardised residuals:

```{r}
Q_BS <- quantile(Us, probs=c(0.025,0.975))
Q_Norm <- qnorm(c(0.025,0.975), mean=mean(Us), sd=sd(Us))
print(round(rbind(Q_BS, Q_Norm), 3))
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
This reflects the downward shift in the prediction intervals seen in the plot.

## Remarks
<blue>Why didn't we do a normality test, even if there is one?</blue>

It is quite common to see formal hypothesis tests for normality (e.g. Jarque-Bera tests) being applied in this type of data analysis.

  - They are not that useful in practice.
  - Because we know that no data is ever exactly normally distributed <teal>$\to$ $H_0$: Normality is (almost always technically) false</teal>.
  
<blue>What matters more $\to$ Does the distribution of the standardised residuals materially influence forecasts and prediction intervals?</blue>

  - Quantiles and bootstrapping provide direct, practical ways to assess this impact.
  - Skewness, kurtosis, and formal normality tests offer little practical insight for this purpose.
:::
